knowledgeAnswers.rationale: A lead with exposed copper or cut sheath is a shock and fire risk. Taping it is not an acceptable control, and the damaged item must be removed from service and recorded.
Fuel vapour near a hot engine or a running engine is a fire risk. Refuelling must wait until the engine is off and cool, with no ignition sources nearby.
A swollen, warm battery can go into thermal runaway. It must come out of use, be moved to a safe area and be reported. Charging or disposing of it in general waste are both unsafe.

practicalCriteria: Given a supplied set of three leads, one battery and one fuel container, the learner identifies each defect and tags the defective items within the assessor's set time.
The learner states, without prompting, that mains wiring defects are referred to a licence holder and does not attempt a repair.
The learner refuels a supplied engine with the engine switched off and the spill tray in place, and wipes any spill before restart.
passRule: 80% on knowledge checks; practical sign-off separate
evidenceRequired: Completed inspection checklist for the supplied leads, battery and fuel container, signed by the assessor.
Assessor observation record for the refuelling demonstration, including the engine state and spill tray use.
Referral record for the mains wiring scenario.
stopWorkCriteria: Any attempt to repair a mains lead, switchboard or fixed wiring during the assessment.
Refuelling or starting a hot engine, or any fuel leak near an ignition source.
Charging a battery that shows swelling, heat or cracks.
